claim: A field experiment was conducted in the dry season of 2017 (January-May) at the International Rice Research Institute in Los Baños, Laguna, Philippines.
source: We conducted a field experiment in the dry season of 2017 (January-May) at the International Rice Research Institute in Los Baños, Laguna, Philippines.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the location and timing of the field experiment.

claim: Three replicates of each accession were planted separately in a normal wet paddy field and a field with moderate salinity stress (6 dSm–1).
source: Three replicates of each accession were planted separately in a normal wet paddy field as well as a similar field in which plants were exposed to moderate salinity stress (salt levels maintained at 6 dSm–1) maintained until maturity.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design with specific salt concentration.

claim: Average fecundity was significantly lower in the saline field than in normal conditions (two-tailed paired t-test p=1.658 x 10–8).
source: Average fecundity was significantly lower in the saline field than in normal conditions (Figure 1a; two-tailed paired t-test p=1.658 x 10–8)
evidence: Statistical test results and figure reference support this finding.

claim: Most genotypes (n=94) had significantly lower fecundity in the saline field (one-sample proportion test p=3.639 x 10–7).
source: with most of genotypes having significantly lower fecundity in the saline field (n=94; one-sample proportion test p=3.639 x 10–7).
evidence: Statistical test results support this claim about genotype-specific responses.

claim: mRNA levels were measured in leaf blades from 780 plants (130 accessions in triplicates for each environment) via 3'-end-biased mRNA sequencing.
source: To examine gene expression in the field, mRNA levels were measured in leaf blades from 780 plants (130 accessions in triplicates for each environment) via 3'-end-biased mRNA sequencing (Meyer et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology and cites the sequencing protocol.

claim: Leaf blades were sampled 38 days after sowing (DAS), corresponding to 7 days of plants being exposed to stress in the saline field.
source: Leaf blades were sampled 38 days after sowing (DAS), corresponding to 7 days of plants being exposed to stress in the saline field.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the timing of tissue sampling.

claim: At a conservative false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.001, all but 3 transcripts displayed a significant genotype effect.
source: At a conservative false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.001, all but 3 transcripts displayed a significant genotype effect, indicating that expression levels of most transcripts are heritable.
evidence: Statistical analysis results are directly stated.

claim: The median broad-sense heritability (H2) of gene expression levels was 0.53 (range of 0.012–0.987).
source: This effect of genotype is reflected in the broad-sense heritability (H2) distribution of gene expression levels (Figure 1b), which had a median value H2=0.53 (range of 0.012–0.987; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Heritability values are provided with figure reference.

claim: 16,371 transcripts had a significant G×E term, indicating that for many transcripts, genotypes showed heritably different levels of expression in different environments.
source: In addition to the high levels of heritability, 16,371 transcripts had a significant G×E term, indicating that for many transcripts, genotypes showed heritably different levels of expression in different environments.
evidence: Statistical results from ANOVA are directly stated.

claim: There was no evidence of genotype-dependent plasticity in fitness (G×E for fitness p=0.49).
source: Although we see a widespread heritable plastic response in gene expression, we found no evidence of genotype-dependent plasticity in fitness (G×E for fitness p=0.49; Figure 1a)
evidence: Statistical test result is provided with figure reference.

claim: Only 254 transcripts showed significant variation due to environment (E), indicating genotype-independent plasticity in gene expression for only a small fraction of genes.
source: Furthermore, only a relatively small number of transcripts (254) showed significant variation due to E, indicating genotype-independent plasticity in gene expression for only a small fraction of genes.
evidence: The number of transcripts with environment effects is directly stated.

claim: Most transcripts were nearly neutral (|S|<0.1) in both the normal and saline environments.
source: Most transcripts were (nearly) neutral (|S|<0.1) in both the normal and saline environments (Figure 1c).
evidence: Selection analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: In the normal environment, there was a general trend towards stronger positive (9654 transcripts with S>0) compared to negative (8,415 transcripts with S<0) selection on gene expression (Mann-Whitney U-test, normal: p=3.95 x 10–15).
source: Additionally, within the normal environment, there was a general trend towards stronger positive (9654 transcripts with S>0) compared to negative (8,415 transcripts with S<0) selection on gene expression, indicating that higher expression of transcribed genes is associated with greater fitness (Table 1, Mann-Whitney U-test, normal: p=3.95 x 10–15).
evidence: Statistical test results and transcript counts are provided.

claim: In the saline field, higher expression of most of the transcribed genes is associated with lower fitness (Mann-Whitney U-test, saline: p=0.0068).
source: In comparison, although the strength of positive directional selection was higher than that of negative directional selection in the saline field, higher expression of most of the transcribed genes is associated with lower fitness (Table 1, Mann-Whitney U-test, saline: p=0.0068).
evidence: Statistical test result is directly stated.

claim: Under normal conditions, 17 transcripts cleared the Bonferroni correction threshold, 13 of which were under positive directional selection.
source: Although no transcripts cleared the Bonferroni correction threshold in saline conditions, under normal conditions 17 transcripts cleared the threshold, 13 of which were under positive directional selection (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Statistical significance results are directly stated.

claim: A high proportion of transcripts experienced stabilizing selection (C<0) in both normal and saline environments.
source: We also found that a high proportion of transcripts experienced stabilizing selection (C<0) in both normal and saline environments.
evidence: Selection analysis results are directly stated.

claim: Stabilizing selection was stronger than disruptive selection under normal conditions (Mann-Whitney U-test, normal: p<2.2 x 10–16).
source: This effect was pronounced under normal conditions, with the strength of stabilizing selection being stronger than that of disruptive selection (Table 1; Mann-Whitney U-test, normal: p<2.2 x 10–16).
evidence: Statistical test result is provided.

claim: In the saline environment, there was no detectable difference between the strength of stabilizing and disruptive selection (Mann-Whitney U-test, normal: p=0.514).
source: In contrast, within the saline environment, there was no detectable difference between the strength of stabilizing and disruptive selection (Mann-Whitney U-test, normal: p=0.514), due to a higher proportion of transcripts experiencing stronger disruptive selection.
evidence: Statistical test result is directly stated.

claim: Selection was stronger in the saline field compared to the normal wet paddy field for overall strength of directional selection (Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.012).
source: Comparing the distribution of selection differentials between environmental conditions, we found that selection was stronger in the saline field compared to the normal wet paddy field (Table 1; Figure 1d and e). This was true for the overall strength of directional selection (Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.012)
evidence: Statistical test results are provided with figure references.

claim: Selection was stronger in the saline field for negative directional (p=8.27 × 10–6), stabilizing (p<2.2 x 10–16) and disruptive (p<2.2 x 10–16) selection, but not positive directional selection (p=0.735).
source: as well as for negative directional (p=8.27 × 10–6), stabilizing (p<2.2 x 10–16) and disruptive (p<2.2 x 10–16) selection, but not positive directional selection (p=0.735).
evidence: Multiple statistical test results are provided.

claim: 10.80% of the transcripts showed selection patterns consistent with conditional neutrality, while only 0.28% of transcripts showed antagonistic pleiotropy.
source: We found that 10.80% of the transcripts showed selection patterns consistent with CN, while only 0.28% of transcripts showed AP (Figure 1f; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Percentages are directly stated with figure reference.

claim: The proportion of transcripts showing conditional neutrality was greater than expected by chance and greater than the proportion showing antagonistic pleiotropy (two-tailed proportion z-test p<2.2 x 10–16).
source: The proportion of transcripts showing CN was greater than expected by chance and greater than the proportion showing AP two-tailed proportion z-test p<2.2 x 10–16.
evidence: Statistical test result is provided.

claim: Among the 51 antagonistically pleiotropic transcripts, increased expression of 38 was beneficial only in normal conditions.
source: Among the 51 AP transcripts, increased expression of 38 was beneficial only in normal conditions (higher expression associated with higher fitness in normal conditions, but lower fitness under saline conditions).
evidence: The number of transcripts with specific selection patterns is stated.

claim: Gene ontology term analyses indicated that many antagonistically pleiotropic genes beneficial in normal conditions were involved in photosynthesis and metabolic processes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) term analyses of these 38 transcripts indicated that many of these genes were involved in photosynthesis and metabolic processes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: GO analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: The reduction of photosynthesis in rice under salinity stress has been observed in previous studies.
source: This is consistent with an observed reduction of photosynthesis in rice under salinity stress (Radanielson et al., 2018; Tsai et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies supporting this observation.

claim: SNPs regulating expression of two photosynthesis related antagonistically pleiotropic transcripts (PSAN and CRR7) were identified only in the normal environment.
source: We found SNPs regulating expression of two photosynthesis related AP transcripts (PSAN and CRR7) only in the normal environment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: eQTL analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: Among the 13 antagonistically pleiotropic transcripts beneficial only in the saline environment, a cyclophilin-encoding transcript (OsCYP2) was identified.
source: We further looked at the 13 AP transcripts that were beneficial only in the saline environment (Supplementary file 4). Although there was no significant GO enrichment for these transcripts, among them we identified a cyclophilin-encoding transcript (OsCYP2), which has been shown to confer salt tolerance in rice (Lee et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2022; Ruan et al., 2011).
evidence: The transcript is identified and previous studies are cited.

claim: No SNP was associated with the expression of OsCYP2 in either normal or saline conditions.
source: However, no SNP was associated with the expression of this gene in either normal or saline conditions.
evidence: eQTL analysis results are directly stated.

claim: 13 biological processes were under strong differential selection in normal conditions and 18 processes in saline conditions.
source: We identified 13 and 18 processes that were under strong differential selection in normal and saline conditions, respectively (Supplementary file 5; Figure 2a).
evidence: The numbers of processes are stated with figure reference.

claim: Processes primarily involved in various aspects of growth and defense were under stronger selection in normal conditions.
source: Processes primarily involved in various aspects of growth and defense were under stronger selection in normal conditions
evidence: Selection analysis results on biological processes are stated.

claim: Processes associated with regulation of flowering, cell cycle control and reproduction showed stronger selection under saline conditions.
source: whereas processes associated with regulation of flowering, cell cycle control and reproduction showed stronger selection under saline conditions (Figure 2a).
evidence: Selection analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: Salinity stress has been associated with changes in flowering time and reduced yield in multiple species.
source: This provides insight into the specific biological processes related to changes in flowering time and reduced yield, both of which have been associated with salinity stress in multiple species (Chang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2007; Zandt and Mopper, 2002; Zhang et al., 2022b).
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this association.

claim: Osmotic stress induced by salinity causes a reduction in cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) responsible for cell-cycle transitions.
source: Furthermore, studies have found that the osmotic stress induced by salinity causes a reduction in the cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) responsible for cell-cycle transitions (G1/S and G2/M; Ma et al., 2015; Schuppler et al., 1998; West et al., 2004).
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this mechanism.

claim: Over half of principal components (7 of 11 in normal and 7 of 12 in saline conditions) displayed opposite signs of direct and indirect responses to selection.
source: We found that over half of PCs (7 of 11 and 7 of 12 PCs in normal and saline conditions, respectively) displayed opposite signs of direct and indirect responses to selection (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Multivariate selection analysis results are stated.

claim: PCs enriched for metabolic pathways and biosynthesis of phenylpropanoids and secondary metabolites were under selection in the normal environment.
source: We found PCs enriched for metabolic pathways and biosynthesis of phenylpropanoids and secondary metabolites to be under selection in the normal environment (Figure 2a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Selection analysis results are stated with figure references.

claim: Circadian rhythm was found to be under positive directional selection, with an overall positive response to selection, in the saline environment.
source: Interestingly, circadian rhythm was found to be under positive directional selection, with an overall positive response to selection, in the saline environment (Figure 2a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Selection analysis results are stated with figure references.

claim: Circadian clock genes have been associated with conferring salt tolerance.
source: This is in alignment with the role of circadian clock genes in conferring salt tolerance (Kim et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022)
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this role.

claim: More than 29,000 transcript pairs (involving 1742 unique transcripts) showed significantly different correlations between normal and saline conditions (FDR <5%).
source: We found that the correlation structure for gene expression was broadly similar across the 2.10 M unique transcript pairs, but >29,000 transcript pairs (involving 1742 unique transcripts) showed significantly different correlations between normal and saline conditions (FDR <5%) (Figure 3a; Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Decoherence analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: GO term enrichment analysis of transcripts showing decoherence highlighted important pathways related to plant responses and potentially tolerance to excess salt.
source: GO term enrichment analysis of the transcripts that show decoherence with significant pairs greater than the median (median significant pair per transcript = 12, n=853) highlighted important pathways related to plant responses and potentially tolerance to excess salt (Figure 3b).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: Circadian rhythm genes like OsPRR37 and GIGANTA (GI) differed significantly in their interactions between the two environments.
source: For instance, circadian rhythm genes like OsPRR37 and GIGANTA (GI), which have been shown to confer salt tolerance in rice and Arabidopsis (Kim et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2021), differed significantly in their interactions between the two environments.
evidence: Decoherence analysis results are stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The relative abundance of metabolites involved in energy producing pathways like glycolysis, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and various other metabolic processes have been shown to be altered as an early response to salt stress.
source: Similarly, to manage the energy requirements of salt stress, the relative abundance of metabolites involved in energy producing pathways like glycolysis, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and various other metabolic processes have been shown to be altered as an early response to salt stress (Che-Othman et al., 2017; Jacoby et al., 2011; Yang and Guo, 2018).
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this metabolic response.

claim: Multiple studies have reported a positive correlation between salt tolerance and levels of secondary metabolites and amino acids with osmoprotectant properties.
source: Additionally, aligned with our results, multiple studies have reported a positive correlation between salt tolerance and levels of secondary metabolites and amino acids with osmoprotectant properties associated with lowering osmotic stress (Krishnamurthy and Bhagwat, 1990; Petrusa and Winicov, 1997; Tari et al., 2010).
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this correlation.

claim: Three traits (leaf osmotic potential, chlorophyll a content, and flowering time) displayed different selection patterns in normal versus saline environments.
source: We identified three traits – leaf osmotic potential (LOP), chlorophyll a content (Chl_a), and flowering time (FT) – that displayed different selection patterns in normal versus saline environments (Figure 4; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Selection analysis results on organismal traits are stated with figure reference.

claim: Leaf osmotic potential was under positive directional selection in the control environment but under stabilizing selection under saline conditions.
source: Leaf osmotic potential is a key trait associated with water transport in plants, and which decreases with increasing salinity, leading to low water uptake by the plant. This trait was under positive directional selection in the control environment but under stabilizing selection under saline conditions, which suggests that an optimal LOP is important under salt stress (Figure 4).
evidence: Selection analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: Chlorophyll a content at the reproductive stage was under negative directional selection in saline conditions.
source: Furthermore, we found Chl_a content at the reproductive stage to be under negative directional selection in saline conditions.
evidence: Selection analysis results are directly stated.

claim: Ion toxicity has been shown to reduce chlorophyll content.
source: Although ion toxicity has previously been shown to reduce chlorophyll content (Ashraf and Bhatti, 2000; Taïbi et al., 2016)
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this effect.

claim: Flowering time was under positive directional selection (selection for later flowering) in normal conditions but under stabilizing selection in saline conditions.
source: We also found that FT was under positive directional selection (selection for later flowering) in normal conditions but under stabilizing selection in saline conditions (Figure 4).
evidence: Selection analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: Flowering time was significantly reduced under saline conditions (two-tailed paired t-test p=0.0012).
source: Moreover, FT was significantly reduced under saline conditions (two-tailed paired t-test p=0.0012; Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Statistical test result is provided with figure reference.

claim: cis- and trans-eQTLs (FDR <0.001) regulating expression of 3065 and 3277 genes were identified in normal and salinity stress conditions, respectively.
source: We identified cis- and trans-eQTLs (FDR <0.001) regulating expression of 3065 and 3277 genes in normal and salinity stress conditions, respectively (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: eQTL analysis results are directly stated.

claim: The median number of cis- and trans-eQTLs regulating the expression of a gene were similar between environments (median eQTL per gene cis-normal=14, cis-saline=13, trans-normal=5, trans-saline=4).
source: The median number of cis- and trans-eQTLs regulating the expression of a gene were similar between environments (median eQTL per gene cis-normal=14, cis-saline=13, trans-normal=5, trans-saline=4).
evidence: eQTL analysis results are directly stated.

claim: 49.64% (29,623 of a total 59,669) of cis-eQTLs were common in both environments, as compared to 18.62% (25,528 of a total 137,100) of trans-eQTLs.
source: We observed that 49.64% (29,623 of a total 59,669) of cis-eQTLs were common in both environments, as compared to 18.62% (25,528 of a total 137,100) of trans-eQTLs
evidence: eQTL overlap analysis results are directly stated.

claim: Previous studies have found 48–77% overlapping cis-eQTLs and 9–60% common trans-eQTLs across environments.
source: this result was robust to FDR cutoff (FDR of 0.01 and 0.05). This is consistent with previous observations from studies on other species that have found 48–77% overlapping cis-eQTLs and 9–60% common trans-eQTLs across environments (Smith and Kruglyak, 2008; Snoek et al., 2012; Sterken et al., 2023).
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support the comparison.

claim: trans-eQTLs explain more variation in transcript abundance as compared to cis-eQTLs in both environments (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; mean effect size: cis-normal=0.77, trans-normal=1.04, cis-saline=0.80, trans-saline=1.08).
source: Moreover, comparing the effect sizes of the two categories of eQTLs, we found that trans-eQTLs explain more variation in transcript abundance as compared to cis-eQTLs in both environments (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; mean effect size: cis-normal=0.77, trans-normal=1.04, cis-saline=0.80, trans-saline=1.08).
evidence: Statistical test results and effect sizes are provided.

claim: At FDR of 0.05, cis-eQTLs constituted merely 0.28% (142 of 50718) of the total identified G×eQTLs.
source: We tested this explicitly by identifying loci showing gene-environment interaction (G×eQTL) and found that at FDR of 0.05, cis-eQTLs constituted merely 0.28% (142 of 50718) of the total identified G×eQTLs.
evidence: G×eQTL analysis results are directly stated.

claim: 11 trans-eQTL hotspots (number of unique genes >30) were identified in saline conditions, but none in normal conditions.
source: Through this approach, we identified 11 trans-eQTL hotspots (number of unique genes >30) in saline conditions, but none in normal conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 11).
evidence: eQTL hotspot analysis results are stated with figure reference.

claim: Natural variation in gene regulation under stress conditions may be dependent on a few master-regulators.
source: These results indicate that natural variation in gene regulation under stress conditions may be dependent on a few master-regulators, as has been shown for drought stress in rice and maize (Kuroha et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The interpretation is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: One hotspot, Chr7: 25.9–26.0 Mb, influenced the expression of 191 genes and contains the gene OsFLP, a R2R3 myb-like transcription factor that regulates stomatal development.
source: Interestingly, one of the hotspots, Chr7: 25.9–26.0 Mb, influenced the expression of a disproportionately high number of genes (191 genes) and contains the gene OsFLP, a R2R3 myb-like transcription factor that regulates stomatal development (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: eQTL hotspot analysis results are stated with citation to previous study.

claim: OsFLP has been associated with salt tolerance in rice.
source: OsFLP has recently been associated with salt tolerance in rice (Qu et al., 2022).
evidence: A previous study is cited to support this association.

claim: More than half genes (317 of 524) appear to have a reinforcing rather than a compensatory pattern (two-tailed proportion z-test p=1.65 x 10–11) in saline conditions.
source: Contrary to this expectation, we found that more than half genes appear to have a reinforcing (cis and trans effect in the same direction) rather than a compensatory pattern (two-tailed proportion z-test p=1.65 x 10–11; Figure 5a; Supplementary file 12). Among the 524 cis-trans co-occurring genes in saline conditions, 317 were reinforcing (~60.5%) and 207 were compensatory (39.5%).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided with figure reference.

claim: Genes under cis-trans reinforcement showed significantly higher inter-varietal expression variation as compared to genes under cis-trans compensation in saline conditions (Mann-Whitney U-test=0.002; mean-inter-varietal expression variation compensating = 1.12, reinforcing = 1.27).
source: Supporting our hypothesis, we found significantly higher inter-varietal expression variation for genes under cis-trans reinforcement in saline (Figure 5b; Mann-Whitney U-test=0.002; mean-inter-varietal expression variation compensating = 1.12, reinforcing = 1.27)
evidence: Statistical test results are provided with figure reference.

claim: Estimated LD between all pairs of cis- and trans-regulatory variants for the identified compensating and reinforcing genes was significantly higher as compared to the background LD (mean r2 compensating: 0.33, reinforcing: 0.36, background = 0.056; two-tailed permutation test p=0.0019).
source: This was indeed the case: estimated LD between all pairs of cis- and trans-regulatory variants for the identified compensating and reinforcing genes was significantly higher as compared to the background LD (mean r2 compensating: 0.33, reinforcing: 0.36, background = 0.056; two-tailed permutation test p=0.0019).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided.

claim: trans-eQTLs for both environments had been under strong purifying selection, with the SFS being significantly left-shifted compared to background SNPs (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; mean MAF background = 0.20, trans normal = 0.0936, trans saline = 0.0910).
source: We found that trans-eQTLs for both environments had been under strong purifying selection, with the SFS being significantly left-shifted compared to background SNPs (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; mean MAF background = 0.20, trans normal = 0.0936, trans saline = 0.0910).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided.

claim: This effect was more pronounced for trans-eQTLs regulating multiple genes (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; normal mean MAF in unique trans-eQTLs=0.099, multiple trans-eQTL=0.073; saline mean MAF in unique trans-eQTLs=0.097, multiple trans-eQTL=0.071).
source: Not surprisingly, given their highly pleiotropic nature, this effect was more pronounced for trans-eQTLs regulating multiple genes (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; normal mean MAF in unique trans-eQTLs=0.099, multiple trans-eQTL=0.073; saline mean MAF in unique trans-eQTLs=0.097, multiple trans-eQTL=0.071).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided.

claim: cis-eQTLs in both normal and saline conditions had potentially been under balancing selection with the SFS being significantly right-shifted for cis-eQTLs relative to background SNPs (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; mean MAF background = 0.20, cis normal = 0.238, cis saline = 0.237).
source: In contrast to trans-eQTLs, we found that cis-eQTLs in both normal and saline conditions had potentially been under balancing selection (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) with the SFS being significantly right-shifted for cis-eQTLs relative to background SNPs (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; mean MAF background = 0.20, cis normal = 0.238, cis saline = 0.237).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided with figure reference.

claim: The estimated nucleotide diversity (π) for 100 kb regions flanking cis-eQTLs was significantly higher as compared to genome-wide 100 kb blocks (two-tailed t-test p<10–11; mean π background = 0.286, cis normal = 0.297, cis saline = 0.297).
source: Moreover, for both conditions, the estimated nucleotide diversity (π) for 100 kb regions flanking cis-eQTLs was also significantly higher as compared to genome-wide 100 kb blocks (two-tailed t-test p<10–11; mean π background = 0.286, cis normal = 0.297, cis saline = 0.297).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided.

claim: trans-eQTLs in saline conditions were under stronger purifying selection compared to normal conditions (two-tailed t-test p=0.017).
source: However, we did observe trans-eQTLs in saline conditions to be under stronger purifying selection (two-tailed t-test p=0.017).
evidence: Statistical test result is provided.

claim: Salinity stress induces increased selective pressure on gene expression.
source: We find that salinity stress induces increased selective pressure on gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: trans-eQTLs rather than cis-eQTLs are primarily associated with rice's gene expression under salinity stress, potentially via a few master-regulators.
source: Further, we show that trans-eQTLs rather than cis-eQTLs are primarily associated with rice's gene expression under salinity stress, potentially via a few master-regulators.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the abstract and supported by eQTL analysis data.

claim: cis-trans reinforcement is more common than cis-trans compensation which may be reflective of rice diversification subsequent to domestication.
source: Importantly, and contrary to the expectations, we find that cis-trans reinforcement is more common than cis-trans compensation which may be reflective of rice diversification subsequent to domestication.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the abstract and supported by cis-trans analysis data.

claim: Genetic fixation is the likely mechanism underlying cis-trans compensation/reinforcement.
source: We further identify genetic fixation as the likely mechanism underlying this compensation/reinforcement.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the abstract and supported by LD analysis.

claim: cis- and trans-eQTLs are under balancing and purifying selection, respectively.
source: Additionally, we show that cis- and trans-eQTLs are under balancing and purifying selection, respectively, giving us insights into the evolutionary dynamics of gene expression variation.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the abstract and supported by site frequency spectrum analysis.

claim: Soil salinity causes osmotic imbalance between the plant and the soil, which impedes the uptake of water and other key nutrients.
source: Soil salinity causes osmotic imbalance between the plant and the soil, which impedes the uptake of water and other key nutrients (Hakim et al., 2014; Munns, 2002), possibly leading to acute ion toxicity (Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this mechanism.

claim: Oryza sativa (Asian rice) is a salt-sensitive crop, facing significant yield loss due to soil salinity.
source: Oryza sativa (Asian rice) is one such salt-sensitive crop, facing significant yield loss due to soil salinity (Hussain et al., 2017; Melino and Tester, 2023).
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this characterization.

claim: Rice responds to salinity stress by adjusting physiological and biochemical processes involved in osmotic and ion homeostasis, nutritional balances and oxidative stress.
source: Rice responds to salinity stress by adjusting physiological and biochemical processes involved in osmotic and ion homeostasis, nutritional balances and oxidative stress (Castillo et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2010; Munns and Tester, 2008; Qin and Huang, 2020; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support these response mechanisms.

claim: An estimated ~50–70% of crop yields are lost as a direct result of various abiotic stresses.
source: indeed, as a direct result of various abiotic stresses, an estimated ~50–70% of crop yields are lost (Francini and Sebastiani, 2019).
evidence: A previous study is cited to support this estimate.

claim: 130 accessions of O. sativa ssp. indica were used in the study.
source: To understand the microevolutionary dynamics of gene expression variation under salinity stress, we first investigated variation in transcript abundance in 130 accessions of O. sativa ssp. indica.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number and type of accessions used.

claim: The field experiment was conducted with three replicates of each accession planted in both normal and saline fields.
source: Within each field environment, there were three blocks and three replicates of each genotype (accession), with each genotype planted once per block in a random location.
evidence: The experimental design is explicitly described.

claim: The application of salt started on January 19, 2017, when the plants were 31 days old.
source: The application of salt in site L5 started on January 19, 2017, when the plants were 31 days old.
evidence: The timing of salt application is explicitly stated.

claim: The salinity levels were maintained at 6 dSm–1 (considered mild to moderate salinity stress) until maturity.
source: The salinity levels were then maintained at 6 dSm–1 (considered mild to moderate salinity stress) until maturity.
evidence: The salt concentration and duration are explicitly stated.

claim: Population variance in gene expression of 18,141 widely expressed transcripts was partitioned into genotype (G), environment (E), and genotype ×environment (G×E) effects using a two-way mixed ANOVA.
source: Population variance in gene expression of 18,141 widely expressed transcripts was partitioned into genotype (G), environment (E), and genotype ×environment (G×E) effects using a two-way mixed analyses of variance (ANOVA) with environment as a fixed effect and genotype and genotype ×environment as random effects (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The statistical analysis method is explicitly described.

claim: The significant G×E indicates genetic variation for plasticity, indicating that this plasticity can evolve.
source: The significant G×E indicates genetic variation for plasticity, indicating that this plasticity can evolve.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results.

claim: Both mean and variance of transcript expression vary significantly between conditions (Mann-Whitney U-test, mean and standard deviation: p<2.2 x 10–16).
source: We found that both mean and variance of transcript expression vary significantly between conditions (Mann-Whitney U-test, mean and standard deviation: p<2.2 x 10–16), which means that the interpretation of the strength of selection based on either of these differentials could be misleading (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided.

claim: The G×E of transcripts does not translate to the complex trait of fitness.
source: This could be due to a combination of factors, like gene interactions (pleiotropy and epistasis) leading to little to no effect on fitness, or environment specific genotype-dependent gene regulation (environment specific eQTLs). Furthermore, only a relatively small number of transcripts (254) showed significant variation due to E, indicating genotype-independent plasticity in gene expression for only a small fraction of genes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of G×E for fitness despite G×E for transcripts.

claim: In the saline environment, an increase in fitness is associated with extremes in transcript abundance.
source: This indicates that in the saline environment, as compared to normal conditions, an increase in fitness is associated with extremes in transcript abundance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the disruptive selection results.

claim: The results are consistent with a lack of trade-offs in which the expression of a gene is favored in one environment and disfavored in another.
source: These results are consistent with a lack of trade-offs in which the expression of a gene is favored in one environment and disfavored in another.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conditional neutrality vs antagonistic pleiotropy results.

claim: This change in correlation structure indicates possible divergence in gene interactions between environments, which may presage a restructuring of gene networks.
source: This change in correlation structure indicates possible divergence in gene interactions between environments, which may presage a restructuring of gene networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoherence results.

claim: Salt exposure induces decoherence of gene expression in some transcripts, that this decoherence results from a restructuring of the gene expression network, and this restructuring can allow salt stress tolerance.
source: Our results suggest that salt exposure induces decoherence of gene expression in some transcripts, that this decoherence results from a restructuring of the gene expression network, and this restructuring can allow salt stress tolerance, providing a potential molecular mechanism underlying this tolerance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoherence analysis results.

claim: An optimal leaf osmotic potential is important under salt stress.
source: This trait was under positive directional selection in the control environment but under stabilizing selection under saline conditions, which suggests that an optimal LOP is important under salt stress (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the selection analysis results on LOP.

claim: The reduction in chlorophyll a content is associated with increased survival and reproductive fitness under salinity stress.
source: Although ion toxicity has previously been shown to reduce chlorophyll content (Ashraf and Bhatti, 2000; Taïbi et al., 2016), our results showed that this reduction is associated with increased survival and reproductive fitness, consistent with the general trend for reduced photosynthesis under salinity stress.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the selection analysis results on chlorophyll a content.

claim: Salt stress selects for an earlier flowering compared to that in the normal wet paddy.
source: Moreover, FT was significantly reduced under saline conditions (two-tailed paired t-test p=0.0012; Figure 4—figure supplement 2), implying that salt stress selects for an earlier flowering compared to that in the normal wet paddy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the flowering time results.

claim: trans-eQTLs might be more environment-specific than cis-eQTLs.
source: Moreover, comparing the effect sizes of the two categories of eQTLs, we found that trans-eQTLs explain more variation in transcript abundance as compared to cis-eQTLs in both environments (two-tailed t-test p<10–16; mean effect size: cis-normal=0.77, trans-normal=1.04, cis-saline=0.80, trans-saline=1.08). This further indicates that trans-eQTLs might be more environment-specific than cis-eQTLs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the eQTL effect size comparison.

claim: The excess of reinforcing rather than compensatory effects could be driven by the extensive diversity among rice landraces that arose from crop diversification following domestication.
source: We hypothesized that this excess of reinforcing rather than compensatory effects could be driven by the extensive diversity among rice landraces that arose from crop diversification following domestication (Meyer and Purugganan, 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated with citation to support the context.

claim: cis-trans compensation/reinforcement can arise due to the genetic fixation of compensating/reinforcing trans-regulatory variants, potentially due to epistasis.
source: Furthermore, it has been suggested that cis-trans compensation/reinforcement can arise due to the genetic fixation of compensating/reinforcing trans-regulatory variants, potentially due to epistasis (McManus et al., 2014; Signor and Nuzhdin, 2018), which could lead to elevated linkage disequilibrium (LD) between the cis- and trans-regulatory variants acting on a gene.
evidence: Previous studies are cited to support this mechanism.

claim: cis- and trans-eQTLs are under different selection regimes in rice.
source: Taken together, this indicates that cis- and trans-eQTLs are under different selection regimes in rice
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the selection analysis on eQTLs.

claim: Purifying selection is stronger on trans-eQTLs regulating gene expression under salt stress conditions.
source: and that purifying selection is stronger on trans-eQTLs regulating gene expression under salt stress conditions, giving us insights into the macroevolutionary dynamics of gene-expression variation.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the selection analysis comparing normal and saline conditions.

claim: It may be feasible to breed salinity tolerant rice varieties without a yield penalty under non-saline conditions.
source: Further, both conditional neutrality and antagonistic pleiotropy have been shown to underlie local adaptation (Anderson et al., 2013; Wadgymar et al., 2017), following which our findings indicate that it may be feasible to breed salinity tolerant rice varieties without a yield penalty under non-saline conditions, though further work is needed to verify this.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conditional neutrality results with citations to support the context.

claim: Different types of stress may either constrain or facilitate the response to selection.
source: This finding contrasts with prior work in rice under dry and wet conditions that found a lack of constraint in response to selection for most traits except seed size because direct and indirect responses to selection were largely similar (Calic et al., 2022), indicating that different types of stress may either constrain or facilitate the response to selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing results to previous work with citation.

claim: Continuous exposure to soil salinity may lead to a tentative increase in expression of circadian clock genes.
source: This is in alignment with the role of circadian clock genes in conferring salt tolerance (Kim et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022), and indicates a tentative increase in expression of circadian clock genes with continuous exposure to soil salinity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the selection results on circadian rhythm with citations.

claim: Responses to salt stress may alter the expression patterns of genes in the circadian rhythm network, leading to decoherence.
source: These findings make sense in light of the fact that circadian rhythm has been shown to regulate salt tolerance and flowering time in rice (Liang et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021), so responses to salt stress may alter the expression patterns of genes in the circadian rhythm network, leading to decoherence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoherence results with citations.

claim: Detection of population-level correlations are temporally biased and may fail to detect the transient environmentally responsive links resulting in false negatives.
source: But as is with such analyses, detection of population-level correlations are temporally biased and may fail to detect the transient environmentally responsive links resulting in false negatives (Cai and Des Marais, 2023) and leading to the failure to detect temporally key processes.
evidence: This is a caveat about the analysis method with citation.

claim: These loci (OsCYP2, PSAN, CRR7, OsFLP) are possible new targets for functional and translational studies of salinity stress in rice.
source: Together, these loci are possible new targets for functional and translational studies of salinity stress in rice.
evidence: This is a conclusion about potential applications of the findings.

claim: Domesticated rice is primarily classified into two distinct genetic subgroups, O. sativa ssp. indica and O. sativa ssp. japonica.
source: Domesticated rice is primarily classified into two distinct genetic subgroups, O. sativa ssp. indica and O. sativa ssp. japonica. These subgroups are grown in sympatry and are often recognized as subspecies, given the reproductive barriers between them (Nadir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is background information with citation.

claim: A widely accepted classification consists of genetically distinct varietal groups namely, indica, aus/circum-aus, aromatic/circum-basmati, tropical japonica, and temperate japonica.
source: Further analyses have identified a widely accepted classification consisting of genetically distinct varietal groups namely, indica, aus/circum-aus, aromatic/circum-basmati, tropical japonica, and temperate japonica (Garris et al., 2005).
evidence: This is background information with citation.

claim: A total of 130 O. sativa ssp. indica (including indica and circum-aus groups) and 65 O. sativa ssp. japonica accessions were selected for the study.
source: For this study, a total of 130 O. sativa ssp. indica (including indica and circum-aus groups) and 65 O. sativa ssp. japonica (including circum-basmati, tropical japonica, and temperate japonica) accessions were selected, including traditional varieties/landraces and three additionally replicated salt-sensitive and -tolerant test varieties.
evidence: The plant material selection is explicitly described.

claim: Seeds were obtained from the International Rice Genebank Collection (IRGC) at IRRI and from a 2016 bulk seed collection.
source: Seeds were obtained from the International Rice Genebank Collection (IRGC) at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines, and from a 2016 bulk seed collection obtained from plants grown under normal (wet and non-saline) conditions at IRRI during the course of a previous study (Groen et al., 2020).
evidence: The seed source is explicitly described with citation.

claim: Seeds were sown on December 16, 2016, and seedlings were transplanted into the experimental fields at 17 days after sowing on January 5, 2017.

evidence: The timing of planting is explicitly stated.

claim: Each plant was planted in a single-row with 0.2-m × 0.2-m spacing between them for a total of one focal plant and seven neighboring plants per plot.
source: Each plant was planted in a single-row with 0.2-m × 0.2-m spacing between them for a total of one focal plant and seven neighboring plants (included in the experiment) per plot.
evidence: The planting design is explicitly described.

claim: The EC levels were recorded twice per day until reaching an EC = 6 dSm–1 and then recorded daily.
source: The EC levels were recorded twice per day until reaching an EC = 6 dSm–1 and then recorded daily.
evidence: The monitoring protocol is explicitly described.

claim: Total RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Plant Mini Kit according to manufacturer's protocol.

claim: The resulting cDNA libraries were sequenced at the NYU Genomics Core on an Illumina NextSeq 500 with the configuration HighOutput 1x75 base pairs.
source: The resulting cDNA libraries were then quantified on an Agilent BioAnalyzer and sequenced at the NYU Genomics Core on an Illumina NextSeq 500 with the configuration HighOutput 1x75 base pairs (bp) and the settings: Read 1 of 20 bp (bases 1–12, well barcode; bases 13–20, unique molecular identifier [UMI]) and Read 2 of 50 bp.

claim: Raw sequence reads have been submitted to the SRA (BioProject PRJNA1010833).
source: Raw sequence reads have been submitted to the SRA (BioProject PRJNA1010833).

source: Briefly, Drop-seq tools v1.12 (RRID:SCR_018142; https://github.com/broadinstitute/Drop-seq) and Picard tools v2.9.0 (https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/) were used to generate the metadata.
evidence: The data processing tools are explicitly described.

claim: The reference genome, Nipponbare IRGSP 1.0, and annotations were indexed with STAR v020201.
source: The reference genome, Nipponbare IRGSP 1.0 (ftp://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/001/433/935/GCF_001433935.1_IRGSP-1.0), and annotations were indexed with STAR v020201 (Dobin et al., 2013).

claim: Broad-sense heritability was estimated as H2 = σ2G /(σ2G + σ2GE/e + σ2E/re).
source: Broad-sense heritability was estimated as H2 = σ2G /(σ2G + σ2GE/e + σ2E/re), with σ2G, σ2E and σ2GE as the variance explained due to G, E, and G×E; e and r represent the number of environments and number of replicates per environment, respectively.
evidence: The heritability calculation formula is explicitly provided.

claim: Fitness was estimated as fecundity, which was the total number of filled rice grains per individual.
source: Fitness was estimated as fecundity, which was the total number of filled rice grains per individual.
evidence: The fitness measure is explicitly defined.

claim: Unstandardized linear selection differentials (S) on gene expression were estimated as coefficients of linear regression with fecundity as the dependent variable.
source: Unstandardized linear selection differentials (S) on gene expression were estimated as coefficients of linear regression with fecundity as the dependent variable in each regression and transcript abundance and block as the independent variables.
evidence: The selection differential calculation method is explicitly described.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on transcript abundance using the prcomp function in R.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on transcript abundance using the prcomp function in R (R Development Core Team, 2013; Kassambara, 2017) and PCs explaining over 0.5% of variance in each environment were chosen for multivariate selection analyses.

claim: Gene Ontology (GO) term annotations for rice genes/transcripts were downloaded from Monocots PLAZA 5.0.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) term annotations for rice genes/transcripts were downloaded from Monocots PLAZA 5.0 (Van Bel et al., 2022).

source: Raw FASTQ files were downloaded from the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) website under BioProject PRJEB6180 for 14 accessions (Wang et al., 2018) and under Bioprojects PRJNA422249 and PRJNA557122 for 92 accessions (Gutaker et al., 2020; Supplementary file 13).

claim: trans-eQTLs were defined as being on a different chromosome or at least 1 Mb away from a gene under its influence on the same chromosome; cis-eQTLs were defined as <100 kb away from an associated gene.
source: Due to long stretches of homozygosity attributed to the highly inbred nature of rice, trans-eQTLs were defined as being on a different chromosome or at least 1 Mb away from a gene under its influence on the same chromosome; cis-eQTLs were defined as <100 kb away from an associated gene.
evidence: The eQTL classification criteria are explicitly defined.

claim: A lead SNP was identified as the SNP with the most significant association within a 100 kb region.
source: For each gene regulated by a SNP in cis or trans, a lead SNP was identified as the SNP with the most significant association within a 100 kb region.
